checks.original: In 1789, France faced a fiscal crisis and a society split into three unequal estates.
The clergy and nobility were tax exempt, while the Third Estate — over ninety percent of the people — paid almost all taxes.
King Louis XVI summoned the Estates General at Versailles, its first meeting since 1614, but deadlock over voting blocked reform.
The Third Estate swore the Tennis Court Oath, declaring authority came from the people, not the monarchy.
This forced the king to order the privileged estates into the National Assembly.
On July 14, 1789, Parisians stormed the Bastille, the Revolution's symbolic start.
Feudalism fell and the Declaration proclaimed popular sovereignty and legal equality.
In September 1791, Louis XVI accepted a constitution, creating a constitutional monarchy.
The monarchy fell a year later when the Tuileries was stormed and the Convention proclaimed a republic.
Louis XVI was executed for treason in January 1793.
The Committee of Public Safety, led by Robespierre, ruled through the Reign of Terror, a ten month period with over seventeen thousand guillotine executions.
Robespierre fell in July 1794, but instability continued until the Coup of 18 Brumaire in November 1799.
That coup overthrew the Directory, brought Napoleon to power as First Consul, and ended the Revolution.

facts.text: Bonaparte was defeated by the Ottoman army at the Battle of Mount Tabor on April 16.
facts.quote: April 16: Bonaparte defeats the Ottoman army led by Abdullah Pasha al-Azm at the Battle of Mount Tabor

facts.text: The 1799 French legislative election on April 18 resulted in a major loss for government supporters and a victory for the extreme left.
facts.quote: April 18: 1799 French legislative election results in a major loss for supporters of the government, and a victory for the extreme left.

facts.text: Bonaparte failed to capture Saint-Jean-d'Acre on April 24, marking his third failed attempt.
facts.quote: April 24: Bonaparte fails a third time to capture Saint-Jean-d'Acre.

facts.text: Russian and Austrian forces under Alexander Suvorov defeated French troops under General Moreau at the Battle of Cassano on April 27.
facts.quote: April 27: Alexander Suvorov's Russo-Austrian army defeats French forces under General Moreau at the Battle of Cassano

facts.text: General Joubert was killed and the French Army of Italy was defeated at the Battle of Novi on August 15.
facts.quote: August 15: Defeat of the French Army of Italy under General Joubert at the Battle of Novi

facts.text: The Ancien Régime divided French society into three estates: the clergy, nobility, and commoners.
facts.quote: The Ancien Régime was divided into three estates, or social orders: the clergy, nobility, and commoners.

facts.text: The first two estates (clergy and nobility) enjoyed tax exemptions and other social privileges.
facts.quote: The first two estates enjoyed many social privileges, including tax exemptions, that were not granted to the commoners

facts.text: The Third Estate (commoners) made up over 90% of the French population.
facts.quote: a class that made up well over 90% of the population

facts.text: The Third Estate was burdened with manual labor and paying most of the taxes.
facts.quote: The Third Estate was burdened with manual labor as well as paying most of the taxes.

facts.text: The deputies vowed not to separate and to reassemble wherever necessary until the kingdom's constitution was established.
facts.quote: Their vow "not to separate and to reassemble wherever necessary until the constitution of the kingdom is established" became a pivotal event

facts.text: The Tennis Court Oath preceded the Storming of the Bastille in July 1789, the abolition of feudalism in August 1789, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen on 26 August 1789.
facts.quote: The Tennis Court Oath preceded the Storming of the Bastille in July, the abolition of feudalism in August, and the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen on 26 August.

facts.text: The oath asserted that political authority came from the people and their representatives, not the monarchy.
facts.quote: The oath was a revolutionary act and an assertion that political authority derived from the people and their representatives rather than from the monarchy.

facts.text: The oath forced Louis XVI to order the clergy and nobility to join the Third Estate in the National Assembly.
facts.quote: Their solidarity forced Louis XVI to order the clergy and the nobility to join the Third Estate in the National Assembly to give the illusion that he controlled the National Assembly.

facts.text: Five delegates from the colony of Saint-Domingue were among the oath-takers.
facts.quote: Among the oath-takers were five delegates from the colony of Saint-Domingue.

facts.text: The Committee of Public Safety was created by the National Convention on 6 April 1793 during the French Revolution.
facts.quote: the Committee of Public Safety was created on 6 April 1793 by the National Convention

facts.text: The Committee of Public Safety operated during the Reign of Terror, a violent phase of the French Revolution from 27 June 1793 to 27 July 1794.
facts.quote: Reign of Terror (27 Jun 1793 – 27 Jul 1794)

facts.text: The committee was charged with protecting the new republic against foreign and domestic enemies, including the First Coalition and the Vendée revolt.
facts.quote: It was charged with protecting the new republic against its foreign and domestic enemies, fighting the First Coalition and the Vendée revolt

facts.text: The Committee of Public Safety had broad powers over armed forces, judiciary, legislature, executive bodies, and ministers as a wartime measure.
facts.quote: the committee was given broad supervisory and administrative powers over the armed forces, judiciary and legislature, as well as the executive bodies and ministers

facts.text: Maximilien Robespierre was elected to the Committee of Public Safety on 27 July 1793, marking a more powerful phase for the committee.
facts.quote: On 27 July 1793, Maximilien Robespierre was elected to the committee. At this time, the committee was entering a more powerful and active phase

facts.text: The Committee of Public Safety governed the war effort, appointed generals and judges for the Revolutionary Tribunal, provisioned armies and the public, and maintained public order.
facts.quote: The role of the Committee of Public Safety included the governance of the war (including the appointment of generals), the appointing of judges and juries for the Revolutionary Tribunal, the provisioning of the armies and the public, the maintenance of public order

facts.text: On July 14, 1789, Parisian revolutionaries stormed the Bastille prison, marking the symbolic start of the French Revolution.
facts.quote: On July 14, 1789, a group of Parisian revolutionaries seized the Bastille prison in a dramatic act of protest against King Louis XVI. The storming of the Bastille was the symbolic start of the French Revolution.

facts.text: King Louis XVI was tried for high treason and executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793.
facts.quote: At the height of the French Revolution, Louis XVI was tried before the National Convention and convicted of high treason. He was executed by guillotine on January 21, 1793.

facts.text: In June 1793, the Jacobins seized control of the National Convention from the Girondins and established a new calendar while trying to eradicate Christianity.
facts.quote: In June 1793, the Jacobins seized control of the National Convention from the more moderate Girondins and instituted a series of radical measures, including the establishment of a new calendar and efforts toward the eradication of Christianity.

facts.text: The Reign of Terror lasted 10 months and resulted in over 17,000 official executions by guillotine.
facts.quote: Over 17,000 people were officially tried and executed during the Reign of Terror, and an unknown number of others died in prison or without trial.

facts.text: Robespierre dominated the Committee of Public Safety until his execution on July 28, 1794.
facts.quote: Many of the killings were carried out under orders from Robespierre, who dominated the draconian Committee of Public Safety until his own execution on July 28, 1794.

facts.text: The final article of the Declaration was adopted on 26 August 1789 by the National Constituent Assembly.
facts.quote: The last article of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and the Citizen was adopted on 26 August 1789 by the National Constituent Assembly

facts.text: The Declaration asserted the principle of popular sovereignty, opposing the divine right of kings that defined the French monarchy.
facts.quote: The declaration also asserts the principles of popular sovereignty, in contrast to the divine right of kings that characterized the French monarchy

facts.text: The Declaration established social equality among citizens, making all public offices open to everyone based on talent and virtue without distinction of nobility or clergy.
facts.quote: All the citizens, being equal in the eyes of the law, are equally admissible to all public dignities, places, and employments, according to their capacity and without distinction other than that of their virtues and of their talents

facts.text: The Declaration was inspired by Enlightenment philosophers and served as a core statement of the values of the French Revolution.
facts.quote: Inspired by Enlightenment philosophers, the declaration was a core statement of the values of the French Revolution

facts.text: A second, longer declaration known as the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen of 1793 was written in 1793 but never formally adopted.
facts.quote: A second and longer declaration, also known as the Declaration of the Rights of Man and Citizen of 1793, was written out in 1793 but never formally adopted.

facts.text: The Estates General of 1789 was an assembly representing the three French estates: clergy (First Estate), nobility (Second Estate), and commoners (Third Estate).
facts.quote: representing the French estates of the realm: the clergy (First Estate), the nobility (Second Estate), and the commoners (Third Estate)

facts.text: King Louis XVI summoned the Estates General.
facts.quote: Summoned by King Louis XVI

facts.text: The Estates General opened on 5 May 1789 at Versailles.
facts.quote: it opened on 5 May 1789 at Versailles

facts.text: This was the first meeting of the Estates General since 1614.
facts.quote: marking the first such meeting since 1614

facts.text: The assembly was called to resolve a catastrophic fiscal crisis.
facts.quote: The assembly was a desperate attempt to resolve a catastrophic fiscal crisis

facts.text: The Estates General failed because of a deadlock over voting procedures.
facts.quote: The Estates General ultimately failed due to a fundamental deadlock over voting procedures

facts.text: The Kingdom of France existed as a constitutional monarchy from 3 September 1791 until 21 September 1792.
facts.quote: existed from 3 September 1791 until 21 September 1792, when it was succeeded by the French First Republic.

facts.text: King Louis XVI was forced to accept the French Constitution of 1791 on 3 September 1791, turning the absolute monarchy into a constitutional monarchy.
facts.quote: forced King Louis XVI to accept the French Constitution of 1791, thus turning the absolute monarchy into a constitutional monarchy.

facts.text: The Storming of the Tuileries Palace occurred on 10 August 1792.
facts.quote: After the 10 August 1792 Storming of the Tuileries Palace

facts.text: The National Convention abolished the monarchy on 21 September 1792, ending 203 years of Bourbon rule.
facts.quote: The freshly elected National Convention abolished the monarchy on 21 September 1792, thus, ending 203 years of consecutive Bourbon rule over France.

facts.text: The National Convention proclaimed a republic on 21 September 1792.
facts.quote: National Convention, elected under universal male suffrage, abolished the monarchy on 21 September 1792 and proclaimed a republic.

facts.text: The Coup of 18 Brumaire occurred on 9-10 November 1799 and overthrew the French Directory.
facts.quote: The Coup of 18 Brumaire (9-10 November 1799) was a bloodless coup d'état in France that overthrew the government of the French Directory

facts.text: The coup replaced the Directory with the French Consulate and brought Napoleon Bonaparte to power.
facts.quote: and replaced it with the French Consulate. The coup brought Napoleon Bonaparte to power

facts.text: Many historians consider the Coup of 18 Brumaire as the end of the French Revolution (1789-1799).
facts.quote: and, in the view of many historians, marked the end of the French Revolution (1789-1799).

facts.text: On 11 November 1799, Sieyès, Ducos, and Napoleon were appointed as the three consuls of the provisional government.
facts.quote: On 11 November, Sieyès, Ducos, and Napoleon were appointed as the three consuls of the provisional government

facts.text: The Constitution of Year VIII was adopted on 24 December 1799, largely shaped by Napoleon and his allies.
facts.quote: the Constitution of Year VIII, adopted on 24 December 1799, was largely the work of Napoleon and his allies

facts.text: Napoleon became First Consul of the new French Consulate government after outmaneuvering Sieyès.
facts.quote: Napoleon was named First Consul of the Republic's new government, the French Consulate
